Journal of En vironmen tal Psychology (1991) 11, 299-320
A BIOLOGICALLY BASED MODEL OF SPATIAL
COGNITION AND WAYFINDING
MICHAEL O'NEILL
Department of Environmental Textiles and Design, University of Wisconsin-Madison,
1300 Linden Drive,.Madison WI 53706, U.S.A.
Abstract
A variety of metaphors have been used to explain the processes of spatial cognition.
The choice of metaphor influences the development of the theory, and the description
of the mechanisms of cognition. This paper examines the dominant 'computer' and
'biological' metaphors underlying theories of spatial cognition, and develops criteria
used to analyze two exemplar theories. Computational models implement psycho-
logical processes through rules that act on symbolic representations of spatial
information. The mechanisms of these models are based on psychological theories of
information processing and spatial learning, and empirical observations of human
behavior. The biological approach does not utilize a heuristic based solely on
psychological processes to model spatial cognition. Instead, this approach employs a
physiologically plausible mechanism for representing spatial knowledge. Central to
this mechanism is a representation that is isomorphic to the structure of the actual
environment.
Building upon the biological approach, a physiologically plausible model of the
cognitive map was implemented in the form of a computer simulation. This paper
presents two experiments that vary an environmental variable (floor plan
configuration) and a personal variable (level of experience in the environment) and
attempt to evaluate the usefulness of this approach as a means of modeling spatial
cognition. The experiments compare the performance of the simulation against actual
human wayfinding and cognitive mapping in functionally equivalent real world
settings. Within the limited settings utilized, no significant difference in decision
making was found between the model and human wayfinding and sketchmap
performance. The final discussion reconsiders the differences between the computa-
tional and biological approaches and proposes directions for future research.
Introduction
Research on spatial cognition has generated a wide range of theoretical approaches
that typically describe the 'cognitive map' as a psychological process for storing and
retrieving spatial information (Stea, 1969). These theories can be broadly differentiated
by the underlying metaphor of cognition that they adopt. The choice of metaphor
influences the development of the theory, and the description of the mechanisms of
cognition.
Most of the current theoretical work in modeling spatial learning and representation
is based on the computer metaphor, in which cognitive processes are conceptualized as
sets of rules that act on symbolic representations (usually semantic or propositional) of
spatial information (Smith et al., 1982; Kuipers, 1983; Golledge et aL, 1985; Gopal et al.,

1989; Leiser & Zilbershatz, 1989). This approach to modelling spatial cognition and
behavior is often referred to as Computational Process Modeling (CPM) (Smith et al.,
1982). In the CPM approach, the rules governing cognitive processes models are
developed through empirical observations of people engaged in information
processing tasks, and reliance on broadly accepted psychological theories of human
information processing. This approach to theory development suggests that the CPM
approach is not constrained in terms of the mechanisms postulated for sensory
perception, short-term and long-term memory structures, forgetting and other
cognitive processes thought to influence spatial navigation (Zipser, 1986). The
computational approach emphasizes the modeling of psychological processes without
specifying the underlying physiological mechanisms.
The biological metaphor described in this paper proposes a view of cognition that is
constrained by physiological considerations. Rather than utilizing rules as a means of
modeling cognitive processes, theories based on the biological metaphor attempt to
model spatial cognition through the use of lower level, physiologically plausible
mechanisms.
This paper examines the dominant 'computer' and 'biological' metaphors underlying
theories of spatial cognition, and develops criteria used to analyze two exemplar
theories. The paper then presents a model of spatial cognition based on the biological
metaphor, instantiated in the form of a computer simulation. Two experiments are
then performed to assess the usefulness of this model as a means of conceptualizing
spatial cognitive processes and in predicting wayfinding and cognitive mapping
behavior in people.
Theory and research on orientation and wayfinding
Kaplan and Kaplan (1982) suggest that the task of finding one's way through a building
is actually composed of a number of smaller problem-solving tasks that culminate in
finding the destination. Especially in large or complex settings, finding the destination
does not occur in one step. Rather, wayfinding consists of starting from a known point
and attempting to reach an intermediate subgoal on the way to the destination. At each
intermediate goal one can reorient oneself and decide which direction will lead to the
next subgoal, and so on until the destination is realized.
Features of the designed environment can serve as landmarks to identify the location
of subgoals. The more distinct the place, the more easily it can serve as a guide to
decision-making behavior. Kaplan and Kaplan (1982) suggest that locations serving as
landmarks can be functionally significant, or perceptually distinct. A subgoal can
become a functional landmark if it is located at a choice point, such as a corridor
intersection. At such a location it can attain special significance because it is a place
where a decision has to be made.
On the building scale, Weisman (1981) defined a number of environmental variables
that people use to aid orientation during wayfinding. These four classes of variables
include: signs, which provide directional information within a setting; perceptual
access, which provides a view to landmarks within or exterior to a building;
architectural differentiation, which is the ease with which different regions or
landmarks within a building can be recognized; and plan configuration, which is the
building's floorplan layout. Other research suggests the importance of choice points on
wayfinding performance (Best, 1970). A simple definition of a choice point is a location
where the user must choose between two or more directions of travel. Choice points can

Spatial Cognition and Wayfinding 301
occur at locations such as corridor intersections and corridor turns (Golledge et al.,
1985).
Of these variables, Weisman (1981) found that complexity of floorplan layout had
the greatest influence on wayfinding performance. Other research corroborates the
importance of plan configuration on wayfinding performance (O'Neill, 1986; Weisman
et al., 1987). A simple conceptualization of floor plan configuration is that of a group of
choice points interconnected by a series of paths, or hallways. Such a 'node-and-path'
network of connections between choice points contains only topological information
about the relations between places, and nothing about distance or direction (Kuipers,
1983).
The physical characteristics of the environment that we use to find our way through
a building are stored in a mental representation of some type. The psychological
structure responsible for storing and retrieving spatial information is often referred to
as the 'cognitive map' (Tolman, 1948; Kaplan & Kaplan, 1982). The cognitive map can
store 'route' and 'survey' representations (Tolman, 1948), Route representations
contain topological knowledge about individual places and the way they are connected
through experience; the 'travelability' between places (Kuipers, 1983). Survey
representations contain knowledge about metrical relations, such as the distance and
direction of places in relation to each other. Developmental evidence suggests that
people first learn routes, and over time develop more holistic survey representations of
space (Shemyakin, 1962; Hart & Moore, 1973). A basic element for successful
wayfinding is knowledge of the connections between places, since this information is
necessary for selecting successful routes from start to destination, even if one does not
know how far away or in what direction the destination lies (rO 'Neill, 1991).
From Metaphor to Mechanism
To implement a model of the cognitive map, the mechanisms of cognition must be
specified. The mechanisms utilized are dependent upon the underlying metaphor of
cognition adopted by the theory. Underscoring the importance of metaphor in theory
construction, Kaplan (1976) argues the need to move 'from metaphor to mechanism' in
the development of a theory of spatial cognition. This section describes the computer
and biological metaphors on which theories of spatial cognition have been developed,
and discusses two exemplar theories, each based on one of the metaphors.
Theory using the computer as a metaphor has three major premises: (1) a cognitive
process is one that manipulates symbols (Simon, 1980; Pylyshyn, 1984); (2) cognitive
processing is governed by rules that act on symbolic information; and (3) learning
occurs through the deletion, modification, or addition of new rules to the
representational structure. A system using the computer analogy favors symbolic
(semantic) information as input, since this information comes in discrete packets and
can easily be used in conjunction with Boolean (IF-THEN) rules of logic (Hofstader,
1985). This 'computation as cognition' approach facilitates the development of models
based on observed psychological phenomena and theories. Rules can be developed
from theory and behavior to model the various psychological processes thought to
play a role in spatial cognition. This approach can result in the development of a model
in the absence of neurobiological constraints.
The biological paradigm is based on three premises: (1) cognitive processing is not
conceptualized as rules acting on symbolic information, but as a function of lower level

302 M. O'Neill
physiologically based processes; (2) the spatial representation is a structural analog of
the physical environment; and (3) learning occurs through modification of the
representational structure, rather through the addition or modification of rules.
The computer and biological metaphors suggest different mechanisms by which
cognitive processing is accomplished. Two specific examples of how metaphor
translates into mechanism, are."( 1) the translation of perceptual stimuli from the spatial
environment into a format useable by the representation; and (2) the manner in which
activity within the cognitive representation is directed and controlled. These are two
cognitive processes where it is critical for mechanism to be specified.
Translation
The process of the translation of perceptual information has been referred to as
'transduction', (Pylyshyn, 1984) or 'information pickup' (Gibson, 1979). It is generally
thought to be a non-symbolic, mechanical process that can be described in terms of
biology or physics (Churchland, 1986). In a symbol-based system, there must be some
means by which information from the outside world', in the form of physical or sensory
stimuli, can be translated into a form that the cognitive system can use to represent the
information and manipulate it in various ways. Because the means of representation is
propositional in nature, some means must be specified by which sensory information is
translated into propositional encodings.
The media of storage for a biological system is a structural analog of the physical
environment. Perceptual input is encoded as patterns of activation between groups of
neurons at the sensory level. At higher levels within the system, these patterns of
activation can be generalized and come to represent events or locations within the
environment. Such a system does not requires a translation process for perceptual
information.
Activity
Activity control mechanisms based on the computer metaphor typically make the
division between 'data' and 'process'. The data is symbolic information regarding
aspects of the spatial environment, and the process a set of conditional rules that act on
this data. Additional rules are employed to oversee the activity of the various
psychological processes being modeled. The biological metaphor does not make a
division between data and process, instead emphasizing the notion of an active
representational structure (Kaplan et al., 1990). In such a system, activity is controlled
by physiologically based processes that are integral to the representation.
Analysis of Two Exemplars
This section presents two theories that are used as exemplars to highlight the
similarities and differences between the computational and biological approaches to
modeling spatial cognition. This is followed by a discussion of the computer
implemented model developed for each of the theories. Finally, the models are
compared and evaluated utilizing the criteria developed earlier in the paper.
Computational Process Model (CPM)
Golledge et al. (1985) present a theory for cognitive mapping based on the
Computational Process Model (CPM) of spatial cognition developed by Smith et al.

Spatial Cognition and Wayfinding 303
(1982). This theory was implemented in the form of a computer simulation called the
'Navigator' which models the basic psychological components of spatial cognition
(Gopal et al., 1989). The cognitive map modeled by the Navigator has two cOmponents;
and objective representation of the environment, and a set of cognitive processes that
allow decision making based on a subjective representation of the objective
environment.
The objective environment modeled by the Navigator is a suburban neighborhood,
consisting of'plots' and choice points. A plot is a unit of land with buildings, sidewalks
and other environmental features. A choice point is any location where a navigational
decision must be made. There are two types of choice points, those that occur at non-
intersecting portions of the street and those that occur at street intersections.
The second component of the Navigator is a subjective memory representation of
the environment, and a number of procedures that act on this data. This component
models the psychological processes of a person engaged in a wayfinding task. It
incorporates several processes, including a perceptual component, 'working' (active)
memory, and long-term memory (LTM) structures. While Golledge et al.'s (1985)
theory describes both route and survey knowledge, the Navigator model is currently
limited to knowledge of routes through the environment.
The simulation has a perceptual component that reads in propositions describing the
scene at the current location on the route, and episodic information which either
describes the goal location or how to reach it. The most salient objects or features are
passed to 'working memory', which corresponds to the currently activated portion of
long-term memory. The system accomplishes recognition through pattern matching
from perceptual input with propositions stored in the working memory. Recognition
occurs if the saliency of the perceived scene or object exceeds a set threshold.
When a match between an external stimulus and the condition side of a production
rule is made, the action that the rule may trigger is 'primed' for execution. Pattern
matching can cause enough activity to spread to the conditional side of a production
rule to cause that rule to 'fire', executing a process or wayfinding decision as the route
through the environment is followed. Thus, the model also accommodates the concept
of activation.
Insufficient data from the perceptual component can leave the simulation in a
position where it cannot make a decision. At this point, the system can call a general
heuristic into play from LTM that permits the system to calculate a reasonable next
move through the environment. This allows the model to account for the phenomena
of impartial or fragmented knowledge about the environment. Activation within the
system can be from the 'top down', (from general heuristics for decision making stored
in LTM) or from the 'bottom up', namely triggered from current perceptual input. In
practice, the model conducts searches utilizing primarily perceptual information.
Working memory keeps track of the rules that need to be executed within the system
and controls the flow of information from the perceptual system to LTM. Information
in working memory is subject to decay over time and interference from new incoming
information. Information in LTM is stored in a frame (Minsky, 1975), which is a
structure that organizes the features and properties of places within a semantic
network. A frame contains a list of descriptive features, and has 'slots' that hold
information about a particular place or object. The information in these slots is
referred to as a 'feature-property-value (FVP) triple'. An example of an FVP
triple is 'house-color-blue', or 'mailbox-beside-tree', the latter of which shows the
power of the FVP triple to represent the relational properties between places.

304 M. O'Neill
LTM also contains a permanent record of places perceived and actions taken during
previous wayfinding tasks in the environment. Golledge et al. 0985) refer to these
representational elements as 'episodes'. These episodes have three parts: initial state of
the person, direction and movement made, and the resulting end state. Thus, an episode
contains propositional information bound together with a rule for movement when the
state is reached. The LTM network structure is hierarchical in nature. Nodes
representing decision points reside at the highest level, with nodes representing objects
(such as car, house, etc.) located at each decision point subordinate to the place node.
Subordinate to the object nodes are nodes describing properties of the objects, (such as
red, cylindrical, etc.). All nodes are connected by links. The links between the highest
level decision-point nodes contain information on orientation, distance between nodes,
and other data.
The Navigator model also utilizes the process of pattern matching as the basis for
learning. If a number of frames representing places or objects are activated
simultaneously, pattern matching is used to determine their degree of similarity. If
enough of a match is found between frames and an external stimulus, relations (links)
are set up between these frames so that in the future they will be more likely to be
activated together. The group of frames becomes a 'generalized instance' of a place or
type of object.
The computational process model instantiated by the Navigator simulation
encompasses a substantial number of the psychological processes thought to be
involved in spatial cognition, such as long-term memory, incremental learning,
generalization, and forgetting. Gopal et al.'s (1989) approach allows individual
components to be modified as needed. Thus, the model can be calibrated to mirror the
observed behavior of individuals or the prediction of theory. The Navigator learns by
traveling a specific route through the environment, and is limited to representing route
information, rather than a survey representation of spatial configuration. Knowledge
is stored in a semantic network and is acted upon by sets of rules. The model accounts
for pattern matching and activation, processes which are widely confirmed in the
psychological literature. The model is constrained by a volume of data from
psychological research, but is only indirectly physiologically plausible. It describes
physiological processes such as pattern recognition and activation but then specifies
the mechanisms in terms of symbol processing.
Neural network model
Kaplan's (1976) cognitive map theory is based on the notion that the psychological
processes necessary for spatial cognition were formed in response to environmental
pressures, such as the need to find one's way through the environment under
conditions of missing or incomplete information, and the need to adapt to rapidly
changing environmental conditions. The cognitive map is constructed through
interaction with the environment, and with experience its structure evolves from a
route to a survey type representation.
The organization of spatial information within the cognitive map is based on a
principle of association called contiguity, which states that events (in this context,
places) experienced close together in time will become associated in memory. For
instance, as one moves through a building, some places are experienced close together
in time, and others have little or no temporal relation. The representation of many
overlapping routes creates a rich associative structure. These many cross-associations

Spatial Cognition and Wayflnding 305
can best be represented as a network (rather than, e.g. a list) of places. Thus, the
cognitive map represents environmental information through an associative network
structure. The sequential ordering of experienced places is preserved within this network
representation (Kaplan et al., 1990). Within the network, places are represented as
'nodes' and are associated with each other through activity links. These links contain
no information in themselves, only serving to pass activity between nodes, and to
represent the topological connections between places.
Rather than using a rule based semantic network structure, the nodes and links in
this cognitive map are analogous to groups of neurons and the synaptic connections
between them. The idea of learning based on closed loops of neurons was first proposed
by Hebb (1949) who applied the contiguity rule in a physiological context. He suggested
that if groups of neurons, or 'cell assemblies' are activated concurrently they will grow
to activate each other more easily in the future. These cell assemblies are organized
hierarchically. Lower level feature detectors feed upward and cause activity in higher
level cell assemblies, that over time come to represent more generalized instances of the
lower level representations. Based on Hebb's work, the cognitive map is also
hierarchical in nature, containing low level 'place' nodes and higher level, abstract,
'regional' nodes which encode the spatial relations between groups of places. Each
node represents a cell assembly, or group of neurons.
The activity of the network is controlled through the physiologicallyb ased processes
of two types of inhibition and neural fatigue. Lateral inhibition occurs when two or
more highly stimulated nodes compete to cross the threshold for activation. A highly
stimulated node will reduce the activity of concurrently stimulated nodes. Lateral
inhibition is a component of pattern recognition, since the stored, abstract instance of a
place (or object) most resembling the perceptual input to the system will become
activated (reach conscious memory). The stimulation of the most likely candidate for a
match will suppress the activity of competing thoughts. Global inhibition functions to
increase or decrease the threshold at which any of the nodes in the system can become
active. When searching for a subgoal between start and destination points, if no likely
candidate is found after a certain amount of time, inhibition is lowered, making it easier
for the system to come to a decision (but increasing the risk the decision will be
incorrect). Fatigue is essential to insure that nodes which become active will in turn
cease activity, permitting thought to move on to other content.
The principle of contiguity enables learning to occur about the spatial relations
between places. The principle states that if perception of place A is repeatedly followed
by place B, the structure of the system will change so that an activity link will be created
between the nodes representing the two places. After the link is created, repeated
associations increase the strength of the link between places by increasing the potential
for activity to pass through the link. This simple physiologically based mechanism
permits the structure of the representation to be altered as the system learns about the
relations between places in the environment, or as the environment changes. This
mechanism also permits the system to anticipate upcoming places along a route within
the environment, since when a place is perceived during wayfinding, associated
regional and place representations are activated.
During a wayfinding task in a familiar environment, if we have the start and
destination points in mind, the cell assemblies, or 'nodes' representing those places in
the cognitive map will be highly stimulated, and pass their activity to other associated
nodes. The strength of the connections between nodes is influenced by the structure or

306 M. O'Neill
form of the environment, and previous experience. The activity passed between nodes
is dependent on the strength of the experiential link between them. During a search
through the network, if a given node receives sufficient stimulation, it will become
active itself. The activation of a node in the network during a search parallels the
conscious recognition of a subgoal between the start and destination points.
This theory utilizes the biological metaphor, emphasizing the notion that the spatial
representation is functionally equivalent to the structure of the physical environment,
and that the representational structure can change with experience. The activity of the
representation is controlled through biologically based processes that are integrated
into the structure of the representation.
The theory accounts for both route and survey representations. With experience, the
strength of the links between nodes increases until higher level nodes representing
groups of lower level nodes are created. Each higher level node is essentially a compact
representation of the sequential relations between a group of lower level nodes.
Research supports the notion of the hierarchical structuring of information within the
cognitive map (Hirtle & Jonides, 1985; Hirtle & Mascolo, 1986). The creation of higher
level nodes within a cognitive map, and links between them, permits the development
of a survey representation, since the links between high level nodes allow the
representation of the spatial relationships between distant locations within the
environment.
Implementation of the Neural Nctwork Model
Because the biological metaphor can explain aspects of spatial cognitive processes
based on physiological mechanisms, this approach is of interest for modeling the
spatial representation and decision making behavior. Given the advances in the use of
computer simulation to implement connectionist models in the last several years (see
Rumelhart & McClelland, 1986) it has become possible to construct a computer model
of spatial cognition that implements the general physiological processes of the
biological approach discussed in this paper.
The model described in this section differs from most connectionist models in several
important ways, including its use of hierarchical structure for the memory
representation and the use of activity control structures such as cell fatigue and
inhibition. This model also differs in that each 'node' in the network does not represent
an individual neuron, but the behavior of a group of neurons, or 'cell assembly' (Hebb,
1949). The cell assembly models a 'recurrent circuit' which allows activity to persist
over time and to spread to other groups of neurons (Kaptan et al., 1990). This type of
recurrent circuit allows a representation of a place or object to occur in the absence of
direct sensory stimulation from that object. Thus, behavior can be influenced by
internally persisting activity as well as from direct sensory stimulation. Such an activity
passing system provides a means of coding objects perceived in the environment into a
long-term memory structure, and for recognition and learning (see Kaplan et al., 1990).
The simulation used in this study is based on a network simulation developed by
Levenick (1985), a computer scientist, to run within a mainframe computing
environment. Levenick's research focused on investigating the operational character-
istics of binary and variable activity networks. The research described in this paper
adapted one of the network alternatives explored by Levenick. In the context of the
present research, it is used to study spatial learning and wayfinding within the built

Spatial Cognition and Wayfinding 307
environment. The simulation implements many of the physiological mechanisms
thought to underlie the processes of spatial cognition. The mechanisms of this version
of the simulation are based on Hebb's (1949) work on recurrent circuits, Kaplan and
Kaplan's (1982) cognitive map theory, neurophysiological data, and some speculation
about the neurophysiological processes of the brain.
Operation of NAPS-PC
For the present research, Levenick's (1985) simulation was rewritten in the Turbo-
Pascal programming language and modified in numerous other ways during testing
and development. The modified version of this simulation is called 'NAPS-PC'
(Network Activity Processing Simulator-'PC' microcomputer version). NAPS-PC has
two parts; a 'builder' and a 'searcher'. The builder receives a description of the
environment consisting of a list of choice points in the order in which they would be
passed through by an observer actually walking through the environment. The builder
creates a cognitive map, which is a subjective representation of the objective
environment. The searcher uses the information in this cognitive map to solve
wayfinding tasks (searches through the network).
The builder
In order to use NAPS-PC to simulate a particular environment, the layout of that
environment must first be schematized by identifying the choice points as shown by the
leftmost drawing of a simplified floor plan within Figure 1.
Next, a list of choice points must be developed that describes all possible connections
between locations (see middle drawing, Figure 1). The number at the start of each line
indicates the number of times each path is traversed. In a normal simulation run, each
sequence of locations are traversed in both directions. Because the version of NAPS-
PC described in this paper does not model short-term memory, the order of
presentation of the sequences of choice points does not influence the way the
simulation learns about the environment. From this textual list of places, the
simulation builds a network representation of the spatial relationships between places
in the setting (rightmost drawing in Figure 1). The network preserves the topological
relationships between the choice points. Thus, in terms of topological configuration,
the representation is functionally equivalent to the layout of the actual environment.
The usefulness of the cognitive map is directly influenced by the number of presentations
of the choice point sequences to the simulation, and by the topological complexity of
the environment.
The searcher

conducted through it. The mechanisms for initiating and controlling activity in the

network during a search are constrained by general observations about the physiology
of the brain. Activity is propagated through the network through variably active nodes
and links. The activity of nodes is specified through three sets of parameters" maximum
and minimum activity, threshold for activation, and initial activity. These values can
range from O-100, and are thought of as percentages of a maximum value. Different
nodes within the network can have different values. The links between nodes are also
variable in activity, and can assume values between 0 and 100. The method used to
propagate activity is very simple. For example, assume three nodes; 'A', 'B', and 'C' are
linked to node 'X'. The links each have a value of 40. The activity level of A = 30,
B = 40, and C = 50. Their influence on node X is (30 + 40 + 50)'40/100 = 4"8. If the
activity of node X is currently 50, its activity at the next time step would be 54.8. If the
activity threshold of node X was set at 75, it will be 'turned on', or activated when this
value is reached. When a node is activated, it means it has been selected as a subgoal
during a search, and it will begin to act as a 'feedback unit', passing activity to other
related nodes in the network. To initiate a search, the nodes representing start and goal
points are stimulated to their maximum activity and this activity spreads from the two
nodes until it intersects (see Figure 2).
If any other node other than the start or goal nodes exceeds the activation threshold
within a certain amount of time, that node is 'recognized' as a subgoal. This search then
continues between the new, intermediate subgoal and the goal point. If during this
search no other node passes the activation threshold, the search is terminated. In a large
setting (one with many nodes) it is possible that the start and goal locations are so
'distant' (in terms of number of intervening nodes) that no intermediate subgoal can be
activated. As the system gains additional experience in the environment, it can create
higher level 'regional' nodes. These regional nodes are represented by the spheres in
Figure 2. Links from lower level place nodes are created 'up' to the regional nodes. Each
of the regional nodes comes to represent an entire sequence of individual place nodes.
With additional experience, links from the place nodes to the regional nodes are
strengthened, and the activity of the system can 'jump up' to this higher level. The
search can continue across this higher level, effectively reducing the search space of the
problem. The psychological analogy of these regional nodes is the concept of a region,
or large scale landmark (Kaplan & Kaplan, 1982).

Spatial Cognition and Wayfinding 309
Control structures
An important issue is the mechanism of control of the various processes being modeled
within the system. While the CPM approach does not advocate the use of an external
process to control the various psychological processes within the system (Gollege et al.,
1985), the computer implementation of that theory does require such a process, in the
form of'working memory', which controls all aspects of information throughput in the
system (Gopal et al., 1989).
To control activity within NAPS-PC, the simulation models the mechanisms of
neural fatigue and inhibition. Although there is no evidence from the work of
neurophysiologists directly supporting the concept of fatigue, it is implemented in the
simulation on logical grounds. Fatigue is a physiologicallyb ased construct, since in the
human system the firing of nodes consumes energy, and the more active the system is
the more energy it will consume. In the simulation, each node has a fatigue value, which
is linked to its level of activity. Fatigue is modeled through a formula that calculates a
node's activity at each time step. Nodes that are highly active will fatigue more quickly,
and fatigue makes a node more difficult to excite. Fatigue is required in an activity
passing system for a successful search to occur, otherwise all nodes and connections
become fully activated and no subgoals will be differentiated within the network.
NAPS-PC uses the concept of neural inhibition to focus the attention of the system.
When inhibition is set high, inactive nodes tend to stay inactive and the threshold for
feedback is increased, dampening the activity of the network. While conducting a
search, if no subgoal is found after a certain amount of time, the system will reduce
global inhibition. This reduces the feedback threshold for individual place nodes and
makes it easier for a subgoal to be selected. Within the simulation, global inhibition can
be biased toward the 'higher' level representations, the 'lower' level, or is equivalent in
both levels. This is determined by the current degree of activity in each level and the
progress of a search. If inhibition is high in an organism, it could reflect a more cautious
approach to evaluating potential soultions to a problem. At lower levels of inhibition,
the decision making behavior of a person could be characterized as being less cautious.
Potential solutions to problems would be more readily considered.
NAPS-PC is capable of representing one aspect of plan configuration, the
topological connections between intersection or corridor choice points within a
building. This model constructs a subjective representation of the environment from
experience with the environment. The usefulness of this representation is influenced by
the degree of experience the simulation has had within the environment, and by the
topological complexity of the setting. The model described in this paper has no short-
term memory component, nor does it model perceptual processes. It uses a simple
Hebbian learning rule to construct the representation. The processes of learning and
subsequent retrieval of information during a search are arbitrarily broken into two
modules. The simulation models the behavior and processes of a person engaged in a
wayfinding task who already has some knowledge of the environment.
Discussion
Table 1 shows a summary of the salient differences between the computational and
biological approaches underlying theories of spatial cognition.
Both models utilize a network mechanism for long-term memory storage. The CPM
approach uses propositional data linked by elements that contain rules and other

information. The biological approach uses the analogy of the neuron and connections
between groups of neurons as the media and mechanism of representation. Unlike the
CPM model, the links used in NAPS-PC contain no rules or propositional
information. They serve only to transmit activity between nodes, and their presence
linking nodes serves as an indication of the topological connections between locations.
Symbolic thought such as 'place', route, and survey representations are emergent from
the activity of the network, rather than being represented by sets of rules acting on data.
Cognitive activity does not explicitly occur through symbol manipulation, as it does in
the CPM approach (Smith et al., 1982; Golledge et al., 1985; Gopal et al., 1989),
although symbolic content can be represented as a result of these lower level
physiological processes (Kaplan et al., 1990). Instead of describing cognitive processes
at the psychological level, the biological metaphor utilizes a physiologically plausible
network mechanism at the neural level that explains higher level cognitive activity.
Thus, the theory incorporates both physiological and psychological constraints.
In the neural network model, a functional analog of the structure of the environment
is created through interaction with that physical environment. In this way it is possible
to model the effects of the designed environment on behavior. The CPM approach also
utilizes the notion of incremental learning through environmental exposure. However,
the rule based approach cannot directly represent the physical characteristics of the
environment. Rather, propositional data encoding environmental characteristics must
be encoded and entered into the system, and rules written to emulate the effects of
environmental variables the behavior of the system. Thus, the system can only react to
previously encoded environmental information using general rules developed from
theory and empirical observations.
The neural network model does not require the translation of perceptual stimulation
for the environment, because all representations, no matter how abstract, are stored as
patterns of activation of groups of neurons in the brain, and reflect an analog of the
structure of the actual environment. The problem of translation appears to be unique
to the computer metaphor due to its reliance on the symbolic representational format.
Such a system requires a 'proposition generator' to translate perceptual information
into a set of propositions (Levenick, 1985). The proposition generator must recognize
objects or places and determine which are of interest to the system. In this way it directs
the attention of the system. The system must also determine the spatial relations
between objects in the scene; 'mailbox is next to the door'. Previously stored knowledge
must be brought to bear to decipher the relations between objects, requiring that the

Spatial Cognition and Wayfinding 311
proposition generator have access to a model of the world containing this information.
There are many propositions from which to choose that would describe a given scene.
These propositions will be relevant depending on the context of the problem and
personal inclinations (Kaplan, 1973). No such translation mechanism is posited by
Gopal et al.'s (1989) model.
While Golledge et al.'s (1985) theory does not specify an external controller that
initiates and guides cognition, the implementation of that theory in the form of a
computer simulation does require such a mechanism (Gopal et al., 1989). In the
Navigator simulation, this 'controller' takes the form of 'working memory', and is a
rule based mechanism that accepts incoming perceptual information, sends data to
long-term memory, and in general co-ordinates the system functions. It is unlikely that
cognition in a natural system occurs in this manner, since the number of rules required
for control in even a simple model of cognition are enormous. Some additional higher
level processor would be needed to maintain the rule base and check the operation of
the external controller. This processor would have to rewrite the rules as the
environment and situations changed.
Kaplan's (1976) model emphasizes a representational system that integrates activity
as a part of the knowledge structure. Activity can occur as a result of direct sensory
stimulation from the environment or by stimulation from other active units. The neural
network model provides a detailed explanation of the mechanism of activity. Activity is
controlled not by an external process, but through biologically based mechanisms such
as neural fatigue and inhibitory functions that can direct the attention of the system
based on the current state of activity within the system. While the CPM approach
integrates the notion of spreading activation within the network, the mechanism of this
activation is not physiologically based. Activity is conceptualized as the execution of
production rules that have consequences for triggering other sets of rules or associated
processes within the system.
Empirical Study
This section describes several comparisons of the decision making performance of
NAPS-PC to human wayfindingp erformance. The decision making behavior of people
engaged in wayfinding tasks in actual building environments was compared with the
performance of the computer simulation as it attempted searches in functionally
identical topological representations of those built environments. Two major areas of
comparison are discussed: (1) the validation of simulation performance against human
performance with equivalent levels of environmental knowledge; and (2) comparison
of simulation and human performance across a range of experience levels within the
environment.
Settings
Three areas within the State University of New York at Buffalo, Lockwood Library
were utilized as settings for this study. Libraries are rich in choice points, have
repetitive, similar features, and lack signage and directional cues. The complexity of the
library offered the opportunity to develop several settings for use in this study. Figure 3
shows a schematic diagram of the layout of the three settings, the relative locations of
the choice points, (shown by the dots) and the topological paths connecting them.
The arrows in this figure show the start and goal points for the wayfinding tasks,

different situations. Thus, a cross-sectional sample of environments was established
that the simulation could be tested within. Number of choice points was held constant
because it was not known if the effects of number of intersection choice points on
simulation performance is a linear function.
Study participants
Sixty-three volunteers, 60% male, with no previous experience in the settings,
participated in this study. The majority of the participants were undergraduate
students at the University in a range of programs, and the rest were non-student
volunteers.
Pretraining
The simulation begins every wayfinding task with a 'cognitive map' already in long-term
memory. Because participants had no previous experience in the task environment,
they were given a pretraining task so that they could also develop a cognitive map of
the environment. This pretraining task is detailed in O'Neill (1991). During
pretraining, participants were presented with a series of black and white photographs.
When viewed sequentially, the photographs depicted choice points and paths
connecting them through one of the three settings participants would later be asked to
perform wayfinding tasks in. In a separate experiment, the amount of pretraining
information presented was calibrated with the amount of environmental information
represented by the simulation, so that both groups could start the actual wayfinding
tasks with equivalent levels of knowledge. After pretraining, participants were asked to
draw a sketch of the floorplan layout they saw, and to mark the locations of the start
and goal points. They were then asked to imagine a path connecting these two points,
and draw that path on their sketch. This 'drawn-in' path from start to goalpoint was
used as an indirect measure of the accuracy of the cognitive map. Research has shown
that topological information derived from sketchmap variables is a viable measure of

Spatial Cognition and Wayfinding 313
the accuracy of the spatial representation and potential wayfinding performance
(Rovine & Weisman, 1989).
Wayfinding task
Each participant then performed a wayfinding task in the actual environment they had
been 'pretrained' in. For this task, participants were brought to the start point of the
environment and ahown photographs of the start and destination points. After viewing
the photographs, they were asked to walk to and locate the goal point. Once they
indicated they had found the goal, they were walked back to the start point, shown the
photographs a second time, and asked to find the goal point again. The path taken was
recorded for both trials.
The wayfinding task for the simulation was similar to that of the human participants.
The simulation constructed a cognitive map of the setting from the imput file of choice
points provided, and then attempted to find a path connecting the start and destination
points. The measure taken from the simulation is the 'Path' (series of choice points
selected) between start and goal points.
Experiment 1
In a previous experiment, the level of environmental knowledge gained after
pretraining was 'matched' with the amount of knowledge represented by the
simulation. This created a baseline at which to compare the performance of the two
groups. This experiment compares human wayfinding and simulation decision making
at this baseline, or calibration level of experience,
Research hypotheses
(1) It is hypothesized that there will be no difference between the path most
frequently sketched by human participants and the path generated by NAPS-
PC.
(2) It is hypothesized that there will be no difference between the paths most often
selected by human participants in the first wayfinding trial and those generated
by NAPS-PC at the calibration level of experience.
Results
Figure 4 shows a summary of the paths drawn in on sketchmaps for the three settings.
Each path has a number in parentheses that indicates the number of people that drew
that path (out of a total of 21 for each setting).
None of the numbers within each setting add up to 21, because several of the sketches
were too ambiguous to be useful. Figure 5 illustrates the paths selected by NAPS-PC at
the calibration level of experience.
The first hypothesis states that the most frequently drawn-in paths connecting start
and goal points on sketchmaps will be identical to the paths selected by the simulation
at the calibration level of exposure. Only in the case of setting 2 is this hypothesis
supported (compare Figures 4 and 5). In the case of settings 1 and 3, the simulation
correctly predicted the less frequently drawn paths. While the settings used in this study
are constrained in size and number of potential routes to the destination, these results
show at least that this physiologicMly constrained model is capable of generating
logical sequences of choices during a search.

Experiment 2
This experiment compares a greater range of human and simulation performance. The
simulation was given a total of nine exposures to each of the three environments and its
performance compared to human behavior in both wayfinding trials.
Research hypotheses
For people, additional experience brings with it increased speed and flexibility in the
number of possible wayfinding decisions. Given a broader range of experience with an
environment, if the simulation fails to generate alternative paths through the
environment, or if its behavior becomes erratic or deteriorates, it may indicate
problems with the use of the simulation as a model of spatial cognition. Because of the
variability of human behavior, any attempt to identify a single path as the only path
people would take through an environment is impossible. Instead, comparing the
routes most commonly taken by people with those generated by the simulation
presents a fairer and more accurate form of comparison. Stemming from the need for a
broader comparison, three research hypotheses were developed:
(1) It is hypothesized that the s~mulation will choose alternate paths as its level of
experience within the environment increases.

(2) It is hypothesized that there will be no significant difference between the range
of paths selected by the model and the paths drawn in by participants on their
sketchmaps.
(3) it is hypothesized that there will be no significant difference between the range of
paths selected by the model and the paths chosen by the human participants in
the three settings.
Results
The first hypothesis states that the simulation will generate numerous useable paths as
exposure increases. Figure 7 shows the path selected by the simulation after receiving
additional environmental exposure. The frequency with which they were selected is
indicated by the number in parentheses within each path. In setting 1 (Figure 7) the
simulation chose three alternative paths that exhaust the possibilities for reaching the
goal point without actually going beyond it. In setting 2, the simulation chose two
paths through the environment. In setting 3, the simulation also generated two paths.
The results shown in Figure 7 clearly support the hypothesis that the simulation has the
flexibility to generate alternative searches.
The second hypothesis states that there will be no significant difference between the

X2 = 0-04, N.S.) where dfare degrees of freedom. Because the analyses for settings 2 and

General Discussion
This paper suggests that a biologically based model utilizing an artificial neural
network mechanism of representation can generate externally valid decision making
behavior in the context of wayfinding tasks within small scale settings. The
version of NAPS-PC described in this paper has only a long-term memory structure
and rudimentary learning module but it can represent a (topological) overview of the
layout of the environment. Once an environment has been learned, the model can
perform searches between any start and destination points. The Navigator model is
limited to learning specific routes through an environment, and cannot construct a
survey representation.
The need to account for mechanisms of translation and activity control processes
were discussed as two key criteria for a successful model of spatial cognition. The
computational process model, with its emphasis on rule based control systems and
symbolic representational format, fails to address translation and deals with activity
only at the psychological level. The biological metaphor represents an alternative way
of approaching these issues. This approach describes lower level physiologically based
mechanisms that model some of the psychological processes of spatial cognition. Thus,
any 'rules' governing psychological processes are emergent from the activity of the
system, rather than specified as explicit rules as is the case for computational models.
While the CPM approach is an important methodology for evaluating the interaction
between the psychological processes thought to influence spatial cognition, it does not
address an explanation of these processes at the physiological level. Assuming that the
instantiation of the Navigator model accurately reproduces the behavior of a real
system, it is difficult to determine how much about the internal structure of the real
system can be inferred. The Navigator models a system's behavior, while the focus of
NAPS-PC is on modelling the system's structure. If one is concerned with developing
physiologically plausible mechanisms of cognition, the biological analogy represents
an alternative approach.
Unlike the computational approach where modules representing different cognitive
processes are developed or modified to reflect observed behavior, the biological model
utilizes only a few simple physiological mechanisms embedded within a single
structural representation upon which spatial cognition can be modeled. Of course, this
lack of modularity makes the biological modeling approach difficult to implement. The
biological approach is constrained both by the need to successfully accomplish the task
and to respect the empirical findings and theory in neurobiology (Zipser, 1986). In
addition, many fundamental questions about the specific mechanisms governing
neural activity have not been experimentally validated.
Some researchers feel that an attempt to implement a psychological theory of spatial
cognition using low level processes to be an unreasonable undertaking (Smith et al.,
1982). This viewpoint encourages the use of the computer analogy as the basis for
developing a broad framework of the processes of spatial cognition. However, the
work presented by this paper suggests the biological analogy may be a fruitful avenue
of research on spatial cognitive processes, since it begins to make the link between
neural activity and overt behavior.
Future directions
NAPS-PC has a rudimentary learning mechanism that picks up information about the
environment quickly at first, and then more slowly with experience. Because NAPS-PC

Spatial Cognition and Wayfinding 319
has no compensatory learning mechanism, its search time performance degrades with
increased experience within an environment. A next step in this research is to develop
an Output compensatory learning mechanism. Additional work is underway to model
differences in choice point salience within the represented environment. This will allow
environmental variables other than topological plan configuration to be examined
with the model.
